reason: Attacked and it held, with one correction to the record. Wording: wist.info/horace/72450 prints this English word for word, apostrophes included, against Odes 3.30.1 to 5, beside seventeen other named translations of the same passage, so it is a labelled translation and not an anonymous drift. I could reach only that one page for Bennett's English, which is the weak point of the evidence, but the Latin behind it was checked independently: I pulled the full text of Bennett's own Horace at archive.org (odesandepodes01horagoog) and found Exegi monumentum aere perennius, Regalique situ pyramidum altius, Quod non imber edax, non Aquilo impotens, Possit diruere aut innumerabilis, capital Aquilo and all, so the five lines the English covers are the right five lines. That archive copy is Bennett's Latin school commentary, not the Loeb, so it corroborates the locator and not the English. Date: WIST labels the translation 1912 and the proposal says 1914. 1914 is right, Loeb Classical Library 33, Odes and Epodes, revised 1927; the Loeb series itself began in 1912, which is the likely source of WIST's slip. Leave the source line at 1914. Attribution: Horace is not in the misattribution list and this is the opening of his own most famous ode. Prose: Bennett's Loeb renders the verse as continuous prose, so running it without slashes is faithful, not a breach of the verse rule, which asks for the lineation of the edition named and this edition has none. Checks: shipped [] and near [] on the full line and on a short opening variant, Horace at 1 for the year from month 3, not at cap, not banned. Format: 73 characters, leads with the name, no dash, curly apostrophes, ends in a full stop, tag Poetry. Theme: the monument that outlasts weather and years is the 'what stays' half of the August blurb. Not refuted.
